To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the EEG is a useful measure of behavioral change in a cognitive behavioral therapy program.

the Imago Relationship intervention program is associated with a decrease in the power of the EEG in the alpha2 (8–13 Hz), beta3 (21–30 Hz) and gamma (35–45 Hz) bands in the frontal, temporal-parietal and pre-frontal regions of the brain.

the brain activity of couples in relationship distress undergoing a cognitive behavior therapy intervention program showed significant decreases in the alpha, beta and gamma frequency bands in the pre-frontals, frontal, temporal and parietal cortices of the brain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method to evaluate the effectiveness of relationship intervention programs.

the development of a non-invasive, inexpensive, and easily applied EEG-based method of assessing changes in brain dynamics in response to an intervention designed to improve communication in couples experiencing relationship distress.
the use of EEG as a measure of behavioral change in a cognitive-behavior intervention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of the study suggest that there is a statistically significant change in the EEG activity of couples in distress that can be associated with a change in the relationship status of couples in distress after completing the Imago Relationship therapy program.

our results indicate that significant changes in resting EEG activity can be observed in the brains of distressed couples undergoing a relationship intervention program and may provide a useful measure of behavioral change in future research.
the Imago program has a significant positive impact on the EEG patterns in the brains of couples undergoing the Imago program.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain is a complex and dynamic system that can be used to measure changes in the behavior of a distressed couple undergoing an intervention program.
the brain activity changes we observed are consistent with the hypothesis that the Imago program is effective in helping distressed couples learn new relationship communication skills.

the brain patterns in the frontal and temporal-pariental regions of the brain show a significant reduction in EEG power that can be correlated with a significant increase in relationship satisfaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
system level EEG patterns may provide a more objective and quantifiable way of evaluating the efficacy of relationship intervention programs.
the EEG is a useful tool for investigating the neural correlates of complex social interactions.
the use of the EEG as an objective measure of behavioral change is an important and promising avenue to explore.
